tldr: Pressler argues that if AI makes language syntax matter less, the runtime matters more, and runs through the JVM's recent and upcoming GC, Valhalla, Leyden, jlink, integrity and JFR improvements.
summary: Ron Pressler opens by challenging the idea that AI suits software because programs are mechanically verifiable: nobody ships long-lived software just because it passes a test suite, since programs must evolve, and no mechanical check ensures evolvability. He grants that syntax matters less than ever, but notes that javac, javadoc and jshell are only about 5% of the JDK; the other 95% is runtime. The JVM's design bet is that a big layer between code and hardware resolves the tension between maintainability, which wants details hidden until runtime, and performance and security, which want those details known. GCs and JITs are optimizers, not overheads, and he quotes Gosling's description of Java as a wolf in sheep's clothing: an innovative runtime in a conservative language.

He then tours the runtime. Generational ZGC (JDK 21) removed GC pauses, shown with a Netflix error-rate plot, and an upcoming JEP sets heap size automatically to balance CPU and RAM. Compact object headers (64 bits) are the default in JDK 27, and the first Valhalla JEP brings flattened value objects in arrays, removing pointer chasing. Project Leyden's AOT cache stores profiles in JDK 27 and will also cache compiled code, so programs start near peak performance. He urges people to jlink their own runtime (about 35 MB minimum), mentions work on single-file executables and 'integrity by default', and praises JFR, which AI agents use and analyse very well. His conclusion: AI is good at self-contained tasks but weaker at evolving large programs while keeping them fast, and the runtime gives AI-written code the same benefits it gives human code.
keyPoints: The language front end is about 5% of the JDK; Pressler's case for Java in the AI era rests on the other 95%, the runtime.
Generational ZGC eliminated GC pauses; an upcoming JEP removes manual heap sizing by balancing CPU and RAM against workload and other processes on the machine.
JDK 27 makes 64-bit compact object headers the default, and the first Valhalla JEP enables flattening value objects into arrays to avoid cache-missing pointer chasing.
Leyden's AOT cache in JDK 27 caches profiling data; the upcoming code cache stores compiled machine code so programs start near peak performance and reach first request faster.
jlink can produce a minimal runtime of about 35 MB, and work is underway on a single native executable bundling app and runtime.
JFR gained CPU profiling, context propagation across machines, and aggregated views via the jfr CLI; Pressler says AI agents get 'spectacular' results analysing JFR data.
takeaways: Upgrade your JDK regularly; most of these performance gains require no code changes.
Spend ten minutes learning jlink and ship a runtime with only the JDK modules you need.
Point your coding agent at JFR recordings when investigating performance or behaviour.
Stay vigilant about AI-generated code collapsing under its own complexity, even in Java.

quotes.text: Nobody releases software, especially software that is expected to last, once it passes some tests that meet some coverage criteria.
It's not clear whether AI makes languages obsolete, but if it makes the language less important, it also makes runtimes more important.

watchIf: You want a 15-minute overview of where the JVM runtime is heading and Oracle's argument for why it matters more with AI coding.
